A city where love is real and may even sparkle and shine, and there is no envy in it. A city where even an old loner will find comfort among people who won’t abandon him and will stay by his side until the very last moment. A city where dreams come true, goals are achieved, a city that has room for everyone—especially for those who are leaving it. And this city is the CITY OF LONERS, a city built for you and waiting for you!

Somewhere in the Fontaine, old hydro archon Furina still trying to find her purpose in life.

For 500 years, Furina played the role of hydro archon. Throughout that time, she always tried to make it look as though everything was fine on the surface, even though deep down she was crumbling under the weight of that responsibility... But now, it’s all over. Now she can be herself, live her life as she pleases. But first, she must remember who she really is. After years of acting as the hydro archon, she must have forgotten who she truly is, what she actually enjoys, and what kind of personality she possesses. It might take a little time, but that’s no problem. Life is now entirely hers. She has plenty of time to find out.

Sooner or later, Furina will find her purpose in life. But in the meantime, she won’t forget to enjoy life. She doesn’t need anything grand; one can find joy in the little things too. Just like feeling the breeze brush against your skin in a windy wheat field...

Furina is still out there somewhere, continuing her journey... just like you...

I hope you too will one day find your true purpose in life. It doesn’t have to be a goal. It might be a person, a place, or even something that keeps you constantly occupied.

Who knows... perhaps one day our paths will cross again. Perhaps one day we’ll find Furina sitting in the same cornfield once more. 

But until then...

It was four in the morning when Furina’s eyes opened. 
 
At first, the world beyond her window was only a blur: dark water, fading stars, and the faintest blue gathering at the horizon. Night still held the sky, but weakly now, loosening its grip with the quiet promise of dawn. 
 
She did not know why she had woken. No nightmare clung to her chest, no sound had startled her, no fear had pulled her from sleep. Her body was tired, her mind even more so, yet sleep had slipped away from her like something shy. 
 
So, half-dreaming, she rose and stepped outside. 
 
The air was warm but gentle, threaded with the smell of the sea. A calm breeze brushed her cheeks and moved through her hair, not cold enough to make her shiver, not warm enough to make her restless. It simply touched her, as if the world itself had reached out and remembered her. 
 
Barefoot, she wandered from the small cabin toward the reeds near the shore. They swayed as she passed, whispering to one another, brushing softly against her like a quiet embrace. Furina stopped among them, plucked one, and turned it between her fingers as if it were something precious. Then she placed it between her lips, tucked her hands into her pockets, and looked out at the ocean. 
 
The same ocean she had seen all her life. 
 
And yet, in that tender hour, it felt different. 
 
There was no stage. No audience. No applause. No judgment. Only the dark silver water breathing beneath the stars. Only the wind. Only Furina. 
 
Something about the world seemed covered in memory. The reeds, the moonlit waves, the blue silence before sunrise—everything carried a nostalgia too soft to name. Not the sharp kind that hurt at once, but the slow golden kind that made ordinary things feel sacred. It reminded her of a day she may have lived, or only wished she had: a day without expectations, without fear, without the need to perform. A day where she could simply exist. 
 
Furina closed her eyes. 
 
For a moment, she could almost believe she had gone back. Back to a time when mornings came slowly, when the future did not press against her ribs, when she did not have to wonder what role she was playing or what mask she was wearing. Memories came only in fragments: sunlight on stone, laughter carried on wind, the sound of water, the warmth of being unafraid. 
 
She did not chase them. She did not try to hold them tightly. Beautiful things, she had learned, could break if gripped too hard. So she let them pass through her, the way the breeze passed through the reeds. A tear nearly slipped free, but the wind kissed her cheek before it could fall, leaving only the ache of having felt something precious. 
 
The world narrowed gently around her. The sleeping city faded, the cabin behind her grew distant, and all that remained was the hush of the sea, the reed between her lips, and the air on her skin. The past could not wound her here. The future could wait. For once, no one expected anything from her. 
 
Only this quiet hour mattered. 
 
Only this breath. 
 
Only this small, impossible peace. 
 
Furina opened her eyes. Along the horizon, dawn gathered slowly, like a secret being told with care. The ocean shimmered faintly, endless and patient, as if it had always known she would come here. As if it had saved this moment just for her. 
 
A place outside of time. 
 
A private domain made of wind, memory, and sea. 
 
She breathed in, and in the pale blue before sunrise, she felt strangely weightless. There was no grand costume here, no carefully made image, no ornament meant to make her larger than life. Just Furina, small before the ocean. 
 
And somehow, for once, that felt like enough. 
 
She stood there a little longer, watching the waves pull away and return, pull away and return, like the world itself was breathing. Then, without deciding to, she stepped forward. 
 
The sand beneath her feet was soft at first, then damp. The sea touched her ankles with unexpected warmth, rippling around her as if it had been waiting. She looked down, then took another step. 
 
The surface held. 
 
Furina walked out over the ocean alone. 
 
It did not feel strange. Not tonight. Tonight it felt natural, like entering a dream she had visited before. Each step sent faint silver ripples spreading beneath her feet. The reed shifted slightly between her lips as the breeze passed by again, and she kept her hands in her pockets, shoulders loose, eyes forward. 
 
There was no destination. 
 
Only the sea beneath her. 
 
Only the sky above her. 
 
Only water and wind keeping her company. 
 
Behind her, the cabin shrank quietly among the reeds. Ahead, the horizon brightened, deep blue thinning into gold. The stars faded one by one, not suddenly, not sadly, but gently, as if letting go. 
 
Furina stopped when she was far enough from shore that the world felt distant. 
 
For a moment, she wished she could stay there forever, standing between sea and sky with no name, no past, no one expecting anything of her. Just a girl at dawn, breathing with the world. But even dreams had endings, and this one did not feel cruel. 
 
The sun rose slowly. 
 
Not with drama. Not like a curtain lifting before an audience. It came softly, spilling gold across the water with such care it felt like a hand resting against her cheek. The warmth reached her face first, then her shoulders, then her tired heart, gentle enough that she closed her eyes without meaning to. 
 
And in that warmth came something like a whisper. 
 
Not a voice. Not really. 
 
More like the morning itself had noticed her standing there, quiet and worn and full of old memories, and had decided to be kind. 
 
Sleep now. 
 
You can rest. 
 
Furina opened her eyes. The sun had risen fully, soft and golden over the sea. The dream had not vanished; it had changed. It no longer pulled her forward or asked her to stay. It simply lingered around her like the final note of a song. 
 
She smiled faintly around the reed. 
 
Then she turned back. 
 
Her steps across the water were slow and unhurried. Each ripple spread and faded behind her, erasing the path as if no one else was meant to follow. The cabin waited on the shore, warm in the morning light, and the reeds swayed nearby like they were waving her home. 
 
When Furina reached the sand, the sea slipped away from her feet. The reeds brushed against her again as she passed through them, their leaves grazing her arms in soft goodbye. She removed the reed from her mouth and looked at the tiny bite marks left behind. 
 
Then she tucked it into her pocket. 
 
A small proof that the morning had happened. 
 
Inside, the cabin was still and dim, holding the last pieces of night. Furina stepped in quietly, as if afraid to wake the peace she had brought back with her. She sat on the edge of her bed and looked out the window one last time. 
 
The ocean was bright now. 
 
Awake. 
 
But it did not feel like it was leaving her behind. 
 
She slipped beneath the covers. The sheets wrapped around her with familiar warmth as sunlight stretched softly across the floor. Outside, the reeds continued to sway. The waves continued to breathe. The sun rested kindly against the window, no longer calling her out, only telling her she had done enough. 
 
Her eyes grew heavy. 
 
This time, she did not fight it. 
 
As sleep finally reached for her, Furina held onto the breeze on her face, the taste of the reed, the quiet walk over the water, and the sun’s gentle permission to rest. Just before she drifted away, she wished again for that private domain of wind, memory, and sea. 
 
Not painfully. 
 
Not desperately. 
 
Only softly. 
 
Because now she knew it was there, waiting whenever the world became too loud, whenever her heart grew tired, whenever she needed to remember that peace could return too. 
 
Just like the tide. 
 
Outside, the day fully bloomed. 
 
Inside, Furina slept.

Sometimes, when you're cycling down a road you've traveled countless times before, a strange feeling appears.
You stop feeling like the center of the world and start feeling like just another traveler passing through time.
The trees were here before you and will remain after you're gone.
The road has carried thousands of lives.
The cell tower has watched entire generations come and go.
And then it hits you:The world isn't resting on your shoulders.
Oddly enough, that's a relief.
There's a quiet understanding in it:Everything is temporary, and that's exactly why this moment matters.
The wind keeps blowing.
Evening slowly arrives.
And for a brief moment, nothing else seems important except the simple fact that you're here, alive, aware of your own existence.
Life is a strange thing.
We spend so much of it feeling as though we'll always be here.
But we won't.
Maybe that's part of what makes it beautiful.
Anyway... we keep living. We keep going. :)

It was four in the morning when Furina’s eyes opened. At first, the world beyond her window was only a blur: dark water, fading stars, and the faintest blue gathering at the horizon. Night still held the sky, but weakly now, loosening its grip with the quiet promise of dawn. She did not know why she had woken. No nightmare clung to her chest, no sound had startled her, no fear had pulled her from sleep. Her body was tired, her mind even more so, yet sleep had slipped away from her like something shy. So, half-dreaming, she rose and stepped outside. The air was warm but gentle, threaded with the smell of the sea. A calm breeze brushed her cheeks and moved through her hair, not cold enough to make her shiver, not warm enough to make her restless. It simply touched her, as if the world itself had reached out and remembered her. Barefoot, she wandered from the small cabin toward the reeds near the shore. They swayed as she passed, whispering to one another, brushing softly against her like a quiet embrace. Furina stopped among them, plucked one, and turned it between her fingers as if it were something precious. Then she placed it between her lips, tucked her hands into her pockets, and looked out at the ocean. The same ocean she had seen all her life. And yet, in that tender hour, it felt different. There was no stage. No audience. No applause. No judgment. Only the dark silver water breathing beneath the stars. Only the wind. Only Furina. Something about the world seemed covered in memory. The reeds, the moonlit waves, the blue silence before sunrise—everything carried a nostalgia too soft to name. Not the sharp kind that hurt at once, but the slow golden kind that made ordinary things feel sacred. It reminded her of a day she may have lived, or only wished she had: a day without expectations, without fear, without the need to perform. A day where she could simply exist. Furina closed her eyes. For a moment, she could almost believe she had gone back. Back to a time when mornings came slowly, when the future did not press against her ribs, when she did not have to wonder what role she was playing or what mask she was wearing. Memories came only in fragments: sunlight on stone, laughter carried on wind, the sound of water, the warmth of being unafraid. She did not chase them. She did not try to hold them tightly. Beautiful things, she had learned, could break if gripped too hard. So she let them pass through her, the way the breeze passed through the reeds. A tear nearly slipped free, but the wind kissed her cheek before it could fall, leaving only the ache of having felt something precious. The world narrowed gently around her. The sleeping city faded, the cabin behind her grew distant, and all that remained was the hush of the sea, the reed between her lips, and the air on her skin. The past could not wound her here. The future could wait. For once, no one expected anything from her. Only this quiet hour mattered. Only this breath. Only this small, impossible peace. Furina opened her eyes. Along the horizon, dawn gathered slowly, like a secret being told with care. The ocean shimmered faintly, endless and patient, as if it had always known she would come here. As if it had saved this moment just for her. A place outside of time. A private domain made of wind, memory, and sea. She breathed in, and in the pale blue before sunrise, she felt strangely weightless. There was no grand costume here, no carefully made image, no ornament meant to make her larger than life. Just Furina, small before the ocean. And somehow, for once, that felt like enough. She stood there a little longer, watching the waves pull away and return, pull away and return, like the world itself was breathing. Then, without deciding to, she stepped forward. The sand beneath her feet was soft at first, then damp. The sea touched her ankles with unexpected warmth, rippling around her as if it had been waiting. She looked down, then took another step. The surface held. Furina walked out over the ocean alone. It did not feel strange. Not tonight. Tonight it felt natural, like entering a dream she had visited before. Each step sent faint silver ripples spreading beneath her feet. The reed shifted slightly between her lips as the breeze passed by again, and she kept her hands in her pockets, shoulders loose, eyes forward. There was no destination. Only the sea beneath her. Only the sky above her. Only water and wind keeping her company. Behind her, the cabin shrank quietly among the reeds. Ahead, the horizon brightened, deep blue thinning into gold. The stars faded one by one, not suddenly, not sadly, but gently, as if letting go. Furina stopped when she was far enough from shore that the world felt distant. For a moment, she wished she could stay there forever, standing between sea and sky with no name, no past, no one expecting anything of her. Just a girl at dawn, breathing with the world. But even dreams had endings, and this one did not feel cruel. The sun rose slowly. Not with drama. Not like a curtain lifting before an audience. It came softly, spilling gold across the water with such care it felt like a hand resting against her cheek. The warmth reached her face first, then her shoulders, then her tired heart, gentle enough that she closed her eyes without meaning to. And in that warmth came something like a whisper. Not a voice. Not really. More like the morning itself had noticed her standing there, quiet and worn and full of old memories, and had decided to be kind. Sleep now. You can rest. Furina opened her eyes. The sun had risen fully, soft and golden over the sea. The dream had not vanished; it had changed. It no longer pulled her forward or asked her to stay. It simply lingered around her like the final note of a song. She smiled faintly around the reed. Then she turned back. Her steps across the water were slow and unhurried. Each ripple spread and faded behind her, erasing the path as if no one else was meant to follow. The cabin waited on the shore, warm in the morning light, and the reeds swayed nearby like they were waving her home. When Furina reached the sand, the sea slipped away from her feet. The reeds brushed against her again as she passed through them, their leaves grazing her arms in soft goodbye. She removed the reed from her mouth and looked at the tiny bite marks left behind. Then she tucked it into her pocket. A small proof that the morning had happened. Inside, the cabin was still and dim, holding the last pieces of night. Furina stepped in quietly, as if afraid to wake the peace she had brought back with her. She sat on the edge of her bed and looked out the window one last time. The ocean was bright now. Awake. But it did not feel like it was leaving her behind. She slipped beneath the covers. The sheets wrapped around her with familiar warmth as sunlight stretched softly across the floor. Outside, the reeds continued to sway. The waves continued to breathe. The sun rested kindly against the window, no longer calling her out, only telling her she had done enough. Her eyes grew heavy. This time, she did not fight it. As sleep finally reached for her, Furina held onto the breeze on her face, the taste of the reed, the quiet walk over the water, and the sun’s gentle permission to rest. Just before she drifted away, she wished again for that private domain of wind, memory, and sea. Not painfully. Not desperately. Only softly. Because now she knew it was there, waiting whenever the world became too loud, whenever her heart grew tired, whenever she needed to remember that peace could return too. Just like the tide. These are the last words I wrote to her

I still remember our look at the burning sky. We stood in a poppy field and the wind tousled your hair. In that moment I lost track of time and felt that something was about to happen that would turn everything upside down. It felt as if the wind was changing its attitude toward us — sometimes a caress, sometimes a push in the back — but I didn’t feel discomfort; on the contrary, it was as if I had frozen in that moment for all eternity. I still dream of the gray-blue sky and your black silhouette against it. A little careless, a little reckless, but real — the one I saw every night. I remember the heights were about to fling down raindrops.
But the drops were on your face. And you weren’t bad and I wasn’t bad, it just happened that way, and now our lives go their separate ways, and every time I think of that day I feel nausea rising in my throat. Then a loud thunder rolled, and I couldn’t hear what you were saying to me through your tears, but without realizing it I read your lips.
And it was then that the rain became part of me, although I became part of the rain; the drops mixed with salty tears, and maybe everything would have looked different if we had pressed into each other and kept that warmth, our scent carried by the all‑pervading aroma of the downpour — but it was as it was. You know, please don’t be sad when you remember me, silly — it’s not worth it. I am only the person who left your life because I had to go, but I loved you to madness and that is what matters. What I have written is not an excuse; it is an attempt to save myself, for you are still my habit, and if I forget you I will forget what is dear to my heart, and that is like death.
Farewell.

I used to have this recurring dream and I’d like to tell it, and if you don’t want a paragraph long comment about a dream I had then scroll. But I had this dream around when I was in middle school. Every time it was the same with maybe very tiny changes. There’s quite a bit to this dream but I’ll shorten it and only tell what mostly stood out. 

I would always wake up in a giant field of grass. Beautiful green grass with flowers and a gentle breeze. I would get up, walk around for a little bit and take in my surroundings. Maybe about a few miles in the distance I would see a giant mountain. On top of that mountain always would be this massive stone “structure”. I always assumed it was a castle but I never really could tell from how far away I was. Anyways, I would always stare at the stone structure for a few minutes, then from right behind me, a young girl would walk up to me. She would stand beside me and I would turn my head at her to see a pale, blonde, very skinny girl wearing a white sundress. She would never look directly at me, instead looking at the mountain I had been looking at before. Her hair and dress would flow with the wind in such an elegant way, almost unrealistic way. This next part is the most striking feature of her, her hair always was “glowing” literally glowing. Like how a glow stick would glow in the dark, except it was daytime. I would stare at her for what seemed like a millennia, taking in her presence. Eventually she would slowly raise her arm, and then gently point at the stone structure on top of the mountain, then in the most soft, calming tone, say, “find me”. After maybe 4-5 seconds of looking at her after she said that, I would always wake up. 

I would say I had this dream about 5 times through the span of about 3 years. I am now 20 and haven’t had the dream in about 8-9 years. I don’t know if the dream had a “meaning” or anything like that, but it has stayed with me for all these years. Not only was it peaceful, but I think when I was in that dream, I had a real sense of “this is where I belong”. Sorry for the long tangent but that dream is deeply important to me and I’m sure almost everyone can relate.

My one gripe with life is that.. there simply isn't enough time. And time passes differently for people. People with purpose see time move slow and steady, each day a journey. Confident and relaxed, time is behind them pushing them onward. They appreciate the little things, because they have the capacity to. Their worries aren't existential. They are actively playing the game called Life, seeing what more they can enjoy.

But then there are those that question their purpose. Question the reason for being born, for existing. Questioning what the point of it all is. Sure, some of these people may be depressed. In fact, most of them probably are. The innocent body despairs at the lack of direction from the soul. But then, some might just be apathetic. In the end these people, we, are all lost, searching for something that tells us to stay. Something that gives us a reason to stay. A purpose to stay. We wonder why we were given these controls. Why we were forced to play this game. Why we are supposed to play this game that oftentimes we disagree with.

The unfairness of time, boils down to the fact that humans aren't just this or just that. Things aren't black and white for us. We don't live just because we are born, just because our instincts tell us to live. Our mind is an existence beyond anything else that we know of. A soul. Separate, even from the brain. The brain is simply a part of the body after all, even if it is what allows our mind to exist. And the body is just a vessel. Our connection to the physical world. Now look, you might be thinking that I sound all voodoo or something, but it's not that mystical. Our mind is our inner voice; our decisions, our emotions, and our reactions. They stem from our soul, shaped by the brain, and that is who we are in the truest sense. Not our body. Thus, those who question their purpose, begin to feel the distance between their mind and body. The body lives on Earth, the mind yearns for worth. We disassociate. We can't just "play". So we stagnate. We go with the flow, doing the bare minimum to haphazardly meet expectations of things we do still care about, without the will to go further. Our souls have standards haha, often unmet though. But going about things that way... It's wrong. It truly is wrong. As someone who's wallowed in despair of life's unfairness, I know this is wrong. It's not unfair. It simply doesn't care about anyone or anything. And that's as fair as time could ever be.

Our body, even if not "us", represents us. Represents our connection to the real world. Our connection to life, where we can take action. And it all comes down to that. Action. Those who take action go the furthest. Those who take action, find their purpose. Those who take action, bring about reaction. As impossible or insignificant, it all comes down to action. Why not pick up the controller? Even if we don't want to play this game of life, why not enjoy it since we're already here? Who knows? This world is vast, the universe even moreso. There's bound to be something, no matter how big or small it might be, that you enjoy. And you know what, that's all that really matters. You taking the initiative and enjoying the time you have with something. It's a mindset, a positive way for the soul. Enough of the social media dooming the future and the world. Enough of yearning for an inkling of fun others seem to have from snapshots of their lives.

It's time to look inwards and take the controller in your hands. This body you have. It's temporary, but it IS yours. Enough thinking beyond our scope, it's time to just immerse yourself for a bit. Have some fun, let go of otherworldly worries. Discover what lies in store for you. Sure, it'll take some effort. But it's for sure better than waiting and wasting your time away. Action. Just remember, action is all that it comes down to. Don't like something? Don't accept it, change yourself. Your brain can come up with something, with your soul to guide and heart to love. Time doesn't wait and neither should you. Whether things work out or don't, all that matters is that you keep pressing buttons on that proverbial controller 'til the end.

This is a message for me. And for others like me who are stuck, stagnant while time marches onward. Sometimes, when you're cycling down a road you've traveled countless times before, a strange feeling appears.
You stop feeling like the center of the world and start feeling like just another traveler passing through time.
The trees were here before you and will remain after you're gone.
The road has carried thousands of lives.
The cell tower has watched entire generations come and go.
And then it hits you:The world isn't resting on your shoulders.
Oddly enough, that's a relief.
There's a quiet understanding in it:Everything is temporary, and that's exactly why this moment matters.
The wind keeps blowing.
Evening slowly arrives.
And for a brief moment, nothing else seems important except the simple fact that you're here, alive, aware of your own existence.
Life is a strange thing.
We spend so much of it feeling as though we'll always be here.
But we won't.
Maybe that's part of what makes it beautiful.
Anyway... we keep living. We keep going. :)

Она навевает воспоминания о далеком детстве. Дальний Восток, деревня, Японское море недалеко от Владивостока. Черные тучи и рокот волн, которые бьются о каменный пляж – там не было песка, только крупные камни. Мне тогда было 11 лет. То лето выдалось дождливым, по телевизору часто показывали наводнения по всей России.

Незадолго до этого я гулял среди затонувших полей пшеницы. Там бродили недовольные и напуганные коровы после сильного ливня. Сам не помню, почему мне захотелось там погулять. Далекий грохот волн привлек мое внимание. Для местных жителей погода была ужасной, но для меня и парней моего возраста она казалась прекрасной, как и любой летний день. Стоя на пляже среди камней, я смотрел, как яростно волны затягивали в глубь моря тысячи мелких камней. Они создавали при этом оглушительный хор вдоль всего берега. Помню, как я дошел до того места, где волны были уже по колено для 11-летнего ребенка. Так и не понял, что меня манило ближе. Я даже не могу вспомнить, как волны подхватили меня и потащили куда-то дальше, не причиняя никакого вреда. Мне было хорошо. Еще из детства вспоминаю, как дед с выпученными от ужаса глазами схватил меня за руку и силой потянул обратно на берег. Я не понимал, что не так, и не сопротивлялся. Дед был напуган, что-то бормотал, но меня не ругал – или я просто этого не помню. Меня отвели домой, заставили принять горячий душ, налили какой-то странный чай и посадили смотреть глупые мультики ни о чем. А в голове у меня стоял только рокот камней на каменном пляже, который звал обратно к морю.

Именно об этом мне напомнила музыка и атмосфера этого видео. С тех пор я не видел моря уже 13 лет.

It was four in the morning when Furina’s eyes opened. 
 
At first, the world beyond her window was only a blur: dark water, fading stars, and the faintest blue gathering at the horizon. Night still held the sky, but weakly now, loosening its grip with the quiet promise of dawn. 
 
She did not know why she had woken. No nightmare clung to her chest, no sound had startled her, no fear had pulled her from sleep. Her body was tired, her mind even more so, yet sleep had slipped away from her like something shy. 
 
So, half-dreaming, she rose and stepped outside. 
 
The air was warm but gentle, threaded with the smell of the sea. A calm breeze brushed her cheeks and moved through her hair, not cold enough to make her shiver, not warm enough to make her restless. It simply touched her, as if the world itself had reached out and remembered her. 
 
Barefoot, she wandered from the small cabin toward the reeds near the shore. They swayed as she passed, whispering to one another, brushing softly against her like a quiet embrace. Furina stopped among them, plucked one, and turned it between her fingers as if it were something precious. Then she placed it between her lips, tucked her hands into her pockets, and looked out at the ocean. 
 
The same ocean she had seen all her life. 
 
And yet, in that tender hour, it felt different. 
 
There was no stage. No audience. No applause. No judgment. Only the dark silver water breathing beneath the stars. Only the wind. Only Furina. 
 
Something about the world seemed covered in memory. The reeds, the moonlit waves, the blue silence before sunrise—everything carried a nostalgia too soft to name. Not the sharp kind that hurt at once, but the slow golden kind that made ordinary things feel sacred. It reminded her of a day she may have lived, or only wished she had: a day without expectations, without fear, without the need to perform. A day where she could simply exist. 
 
Furina closed her eyes. 
 
For a moment, she could almost believe she had gone back. Back to a time when mornings came slowly, when the future did not press against her ribs, when she did not have to wonder what role she was playing or what mask she was wearing. Memories came only in fragments: sunlight on stone, laughter carried on wind, the sound of water, the warmth of being unafraid. 
 
She did not chase them. She did not try to hold them tightly. Beautiful things, she had learned, could break if gripped too hard. So she let them pass through her, the way the breeze passed through the reeds. A tear nearly slipped free, but the wind kissed her cheek before it could fall, leaving only the ache of having felt something precious. 
 
The world narrowed gently around her. The sleeping city faded, the cabin behind her grew distant, and all that remained was the hush of the sea, the reed between her lips, and the air on her skin. The past could not wound her here. The future could wait. For once, no one expected anything from her. 
 
Only this quiet hour mattered. 
 
Only this breath. 
 
Only this small, impossible peace. 
 
Furina opened her eyes. Along the horizon, dawn gathered slowly, like a secret being told with care. The ocean shimmered faintly, endless and patient, as if it had always known she would come here. As if it had saved this moment just for her. 
 
A place outside of time. 
 
A private domain made of wind, memory, and sea. 
 
She breathed in, and in the pale blue before sunrise, she felt strangely weightless. There was no grand costume here, no carefully made image, no ornament meant to make her larger than life. Just Furina, small before the ocean. 
 
And somehow, for once, that felt like enough. 
 
She stood there a little longer, watching the waves pull away and return, pull away and return, like the world itself was breathing. Then, without deciding to, she stepped forward. 
 
The sand beneath her feet was soft at first, then damp. The sea touched her ankles with unexpected warmth, rippling around her as if it had been waiting. She looked down, then took another step. 
 
The surface held. 
 
Furina walked out over the ocean alone. 
 
It did not feel strange. Not tonight. Tonight it felt natural, like entering a dream she had visited before. Each step sent faint silver ripples spreading beneath her feet. The reed shifted slightly between her lips as the breeze passed by again, and she kept her hands in her pockets, shoulders loose, eyes forward. 
 
There was no destination. 
 
Only the sea beneath her. 
 
Only the sky above her. 
 
Only water and wind keeping her company. 
 
Behind her, the cabin shrank quietly among the reeds. Ahead, the horizon brightened, deep blue thinning into gold. The stars faded one by one, not suddenly, not sadly, but gently, as if letting go. 
 
Furina stopped when she was far enough from shore that the world felt distant. 
 
For a moment, she wished she could stay there forever, standing between sea and sky with no name, no past, no one expecting anything of her. Just a girl at dawn, breathing with the world. But even dreams had endings, and this one did not feel cruel. 
 
The sun rose slowly. 
 
Not with drama. Not like a curtain lifting before an audience. It came softly, spilling gold across the water with such care it felt like a hand resting against her cheek. The warmth reached her face first, then her shoulders, then her tired heart, gentle enough that she closed her eyes without meaning to. 
 
And in that warmth came something like a whisper. 
 
Not a voice. Not really. 
 
More like the morning itself had noticed her standing there, quiet and worn and full of old memories, and had decided to be kind. 
 
Sleep now. 
 
You can rest. 
 
Furina opened her eyes. The sun had risen fully, soft and golden over the sea. The dream had not vanished; it had changed. It no longer pulled her forward or asked her to stay. It simply lingered around her like the final note of a song. 
 
She smiled faintly around the reed. 
 
Then she turned back. 
 
Her steps across the water were slow and unhurried. Each ripple spread and faded behind her, erasing the path as if no one else was meant to follow. The cabin waited on the shore, warm in the morning light, and the reeds swayed nearby like they were waving her home. 
 
When Furina reached the sand, the sea slipped away from her feet. The reeds brushed against her again as she passed through them, their leaves grazing her arms in soft goodbye. She removed the reed from her mouth and looked at the tiny bite marks left behind. 
 
Then she tucked it into her pocket. 
 
A small proof that the morning had happened. 
 
Inside, the cabin was still and dim, holding the last pieces of night. Furina stepped in quietly, as if afraid to wake the peace she had brought back with her. She sat on the edge of her bed and looked out the window one last time. 
 
The ocean was bright now. 
 
Awake. 
 
But it did not feel like it was leaving her behind. 
 
She slipped beneath the covers. The sheets wrapped around her with familiar warmth as sunlight stretched softly across the floor. Outside, the reeds continued to sway. The waves continued to breathe. The sun rested kindly against the window, no longer calling her out, only telling her she had done enough. 
 
Her eyes grew heavy. 
 
This time, she did not fight it. 
 
As sleep finally reached for her, Furina held onto the breeze on her face, the taste of the reed, the quiet walk over the water, and the sun’s gentle permission to rest. Just before she drifted away, she wished again for that private domain of wind, memory, and sea. 
 
Not painfully. 
 
Not desperately. 
 
Only softly. 
 
Because now she knew it was there, waiting whenever the world became too loud, whenever her heart grew tired, whenever she needed to remember that peace could return too. 
 
Just like the tide. 
 
Outside, the day fully bloomed. 
 
Inside, Furina slept.

Thanks @yurithnovasyndicate3910 for the beautiful start — here's where it goes next: 
 
When Furina woke again, the light in the room had shifted from morning gold to the softer amber of late afternoon. 

She did not move at first. She only lay there and listened — gulls somewhere far off, the creak of a boat, a voice calling out and another answering it. Ordinary sounds. Sounds that did not need her. 
Her hand found the reed before it found anything else. Still in her pocket, dry now, its edges curling. She turned it once between her fingers, and the whole of the dawn came back to her, unbroken, as if it had never left. 
 
The city would want her again by evening. 
 
There would be the long coat. The practiced tilt of her chin. The voice she had spent centuries shaping so it would never once shake in front of a crowd. There would be eyes on her — dozens, sometimes hundreds — each one expecting the performance she had given a thousand times before. She knew the shape of that evening the way she knew the shape of her own hands. 
 
But something in her chest sat differently now. 
 
She dressed slowly. When she caught her reflection, she did not rush to arrange it into the version of herself the city already knew. She looked first. Tired eyes. A face that had walked out over water once, and had come back only because it chose to. 
 
She slipped the reed into the inner pocket, close to where a heart might rest, if hearts were the kind of thing that could be pinned in place. 
 
The court was loud that night, as it always was — voices rising, arguing, posturing. Furina rose above them the way she always did, sharp and bright and untouchable. No one saw her hand drift once to her chest. No one heard the small breath she took before she spoke, a breath that tasted, faintly, of reed and salt. 
 
No one needed to. 
 
That was the secret of it. That was what made it hers. 
 
A performance could still be a performance, and a mask could still be worn well, even while something quiet and real went on breathing underneath it. The two did not have to fight each other. She had spent so long believing they did. 
 
When the hall finally emptied and the candles burned low, Furina walked home along the water instead of the main road, though it was longer and her feet ached from standing so many hours in borrowed authority. 
 
The tide was out. The sand lay dark and open, scattered with shells and the ghosts of footprints already half erased. 
 
She did not walk onto the water this time. 
 
She did not need to. 
 
It was enough to know it was there — that past the last streetlamp, the reeds would still be swaying, patient, unbothered, waiting for whatever hour she next came to them. 
 
She stood instead where dry sand turned wet, and let the last of the tide reach her ankles once, briefly, like a hand offered in greeting. 
 
Then she turned for home, and did not look back, and did not need to. 
 
Because the sea, she had learned, was not a place. 
 
It was a promise. 
 
And a promise, unlike a performance, needed no audience to be kept.
